Markets Conduct Act 2013 (FMCA). CBA NZ is also part of the CBA New Zealand Operating Group which 
comprises Commonwealth Bank of Australia’s New Zealand businesses.

registered in New Zealand, but with the benefit of the  Financial Markets Conduct (Climate-related 
Disclosures – Commonwealth Bank of Australia New Zealand) Exemption Notice 2024, and accordingly 
does not include relevant information in relation to ASB Bank Limited (company number 398445; NZBN 
9429039435743) and its subsidiaries (ASB Climate Statement) or ASB Holdings Limited (company 
number 428135; NZBN 9429039342768). The ASB Climate Statement for FY24 can be found at 
asb.co.nz/about-us/sustainability.html

Introduction 
This climate statement covers CBA NZ (company number 1046786), CBA Funding (NZ) Limited 
(company number: 931499), and CBA Investments (No. 4) Ltd (company number: 931501) (together, the 
CBA NZ Group).  Any mention of ‘we’, ‘us’, and ‘our’, means the CBA NZ Group.  
• 
CBA NZ is the New Zealand branch of Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA Group), which is 
incorporated in Australia, and is a registered bank in New Zealand under the Banking (Prudential 
Supervision) Act 1989. Any mention of ‘CBA Group’ and the ‘Overseas Banking Group’ means the 
parent entity of CBA NZ. Note that the CBA NZ Operations Disclosure Statement refers to CBA 
NZ as the ‘Branch’. 
• 
CBA Investments (No.4) Limited is a New Zealand company, wholly owned by CBA Funding (NZ) 
Limited, and its activities are limited to revolving tax pool facilities with two tax pooling companies 
in NZ and associated funding from CBA Group.  
• 
CBA Funding (NZ) Limited is a New Zealand company, the parent company of CBA Investments 
No.4 Limited and doesn’t carry out any business activities.  
The audience for the disclosures contained in this climate statement are CBA NZ Group’s “primary users”, 
defined in NZ CS 1 as “the existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors” of the climate 
reporting entity. This is a small number of relatively sophisticated entities composed primarily of clients of 
CBA NZ to the extent that their accounts are in credit, and funding provided to CBA NZ Group from CBA 
Group.  
 
About Commonwealth Bank of Australia (NZ branch) 
CBA NZ includes three business units: Institutional Banking & Markets (IB&M NZ), Financial Crime Services 
NZ and CBA NZ Treasury. There are also a further eight CBA Group employees who work in New Zealand 
for non-CBA NZ Group business units.  
• 
IB&M NZ is the primary client-facing function of CBA NZ and provides Corporate and Institutional 
clients in New Zealand with a comprehensive range of products and services, including lending, 
global markets, and debt capital markets. It has 108 client groups as at 30 June 2024, all of 
which are classified as ‘wholesale’ clients (under the FMCA). This includes government entities and 
large corporate clients in sectors such as commercial property, finance, agriculture, transport, 
health, infrastructure, etc. IB&M NZ has 26 staff members.  
• 
Financial Crime Services NZ has 142 staff members and manages financial crime prevention 
operations for CBA Group; and 
• 
CBA NZ Treasury provides the funding for IB&M NZ.  
The CEO of CBA NZ (who is also the Managing Director of IB&M NZ) is the most senior person for the 
entities covered in scope of this climate statement.

Governance  
This section provides relevant information about the Governance body responsible for 
oversight of CBA NZ Group’s climate-related risks and opportunities, being the CBA 
Group Board, and the role that management places in assessing and managing them.  
The CBA Group Board is the responsible governing body for the climate-related risks and opportunities of 
CBA Group’s activities. CBA Group’s activities include the business activities of CBA NZ Group and 
consequently the CBA NZ branch’s climate-related risks and opportunities.  
To carry out its responsibilities, the CBA Group Board’s standing committees assist the CBA Group Board. 
The CBA Group Board and its standing committees are also supported by various management 
committees including, CBA Group risk committees, the CBA Group Executive Leadership Team, those 
within the CBA Group IB&M Leadership Team, and CBA NZ management level committees. 
  
 
 
As a branch of the CBA Group, CBA NZ operates under the CBA Group corporate governance framework 
and is required to adhere to CBA Group policies and procedures. 
The CBA Group Board oversees the CBA Group’s management of climate-related risks and opportunities.

Once the CBA Group Board has endorsed the CBA Group strategy, the CEO of CBA Group CEO is

Group Executive CBA IB&M is accountable for endorsing the CBA NZ strategy, having regard to the CBA

The management of climate‑related opportunities is primarily a management responsibility, with individual 
opportunities identified at the business unit level. Where appropriate, climate‑related opportunities may 
be escalated to the appropriate management committee or the CBA Group Board. Primarily for materiality 
reasons, there are expected to be very limited instances when CBA NZ Group would elevate climate-
related risks or opportunities to the CBA Group Board. However, if a proposed transaction in IB&M NZ 
required further review, it would be escalated to the CBA IB&M Commitments Committee, which would 
consider the transaction’s reputational risks and alignment with CBA Group’s strategy and values.  
 
CBA NZ  
As a branch of CBA Group, CBA NZ operates under the CBA Group corporate governance framework and 
is required to adhere to CBA Group policies and procedures. This includes adhering to CBA Group 
Strategy, and any CBA Group climate-related goals (where they apply). Where climate-related risks and 
opportunities are identified by the IB&M NZ relationship team, they are reported at the IB&M NZ Financial 
Risk Committee (IB&M NZ FRC). They may also be escalated to the relevant CBA IB&M transaction level 
committee or CBA Group Board if the IB&M NZ FRC agrees to do so. There is no formal process or 
frequency for this; risks and opportunities are escalated as and when required.

who reports to the Group Executive CBA IB&M (who is a member of the CBA Group Executive Leadership

Skills and competencies  
The CBA Group Board assesses the appropriate mix of skills, experience, knowledge, independence, 
expertise and diversity required for effective governance, and the extent to which they are represented on 
the CBA Group Board or relevant Committee. One of the skills included in the CBA Group Board Skills 
Matrix is E&S, which includes skills for oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities. On the E&S 
skill, of our nine CBA Group Board members, four directors have been assessed as ‘high competency, 
knowledge and experience’ and five have been assessed as ‘practised/direct experience’, as relevant to 
CBA Group.  
The CBA Group Nominations Committee oversees the CBA Group Board induction program offered to 
each new non-executive director which is customised for their skill set. In 2024, the CBA Group 
Nominations Committee approved an expanded ESG briefing session for new non-executive directors. At 
least annually, the CBA Group Nominations Committee reviews the continuing education program 
provided to all directors. This helps to ensure there are appropriate continuing education opportunities for 
directors to develop and maintain the skills and knowledge required to effectively perform their role on the 
CBA Group Board. This year, the CBA Group Board continued to invest in environment-related training 
with a session held on the evolving context of nature resilience and risk. This was led by an external expert 
covering the global context, nature as a strategic risk and opportunity, and implications for financial 
institutions.

CBA Group Board has approved interim 2030 sector-level financed emissions targets at the CBA Group 
level. To the extent CBA NZ has exposures that would be in-scope of these targets above, they are

NZ Branch 
The CEO of CBA NZ has overall responsibility for the management of CBA NZ Branch including its 
assessment and management of climate-related risks and opportunities from financing deals for clients. 
They are supported by the CBA NZ management level committees and CBA IB&M governance 
committees, including the Coverage Business Risk Forum (CBRF), CBA IB&M NFRC and the Global 
Markets Non-Financial Risk Committee. 
The CEO of CBA NZ is a key member of the CBA NZ Assets & Liabilities Committee (ALCO), the IB&M NZ 
FRC, the IB&M NZ NFRC, and the CBA IB&M Coverage Leadership Team. They are also a director of CBA 
Investments (No.4) Ltd and CBA Funding (NZ) Ltd (refer to the Introduction section for details about 
these entities). 
CBA NZ management level committees 
The IB&M NZ FRC reviews client deals in the pipeline in the last two months that have either a climate-
related or E&S-related risk or opportunity. It discusses the impact of the deal, and the decision is made at 
either the EDR or the CBA IB&M Commitments Committee (CommComm) (described below). The CBA 
IB&M Financial Risk Committee quorum includes senior staff in Finance, Credit Risk and CBA NZ head 
office. 
The IB&M NZ NFRC discusses changes to the IB&M NZ risk profile, regulatory changes, compliance, and 
key projects that impact the risk environment. The IB&M NZ NFRC quorum includes senior staff in 
Compliance, Non-Financial Risk & Conducts, Cybersecurity, Human Resources, Financial Crime 
Compliance, and CBA NZ head office. Both the IB&M NZ FRC and the IB&M NZ NFRC meet once every 
two months.

Management of transactions 
In IB&M NZ (which is the primary client facing business unit within CBA NZ), lending customers are 
relationship managed and supported directly by our bankers. As part of the corporate lending process, 
ESG risk assessments are completed for CBA NZ institutional customers, and are reviewed and refreshed 
annually. IB&M NZ participates in two key CBA IB&M forums that support consideration of E&S risks, non-
financial risks and other reputational risks in IB&M NZ’s portfolio. These review forums, which involve 
senior stakeholders from within and outside IB&M NZ include the EDR and the CBA IB&M Commitments 
Committee. 
CBA NZ Treasury provides funding to CBA NZ. CBA NZ is funded by and provides funding to entities 
within the CBA Group, including long-term funding from CBA Sydney, and short-term funding to and from 
CBA Sydney, CBA Hong Kong and ASB. CBA NZ also holds some liquid assets in the form of bonds and 
repos. 
Following the publication of the updated CBA Group E&S Framework in August 2023, existing processes 
(which IB&M NZ is required to follow) were enhanced to require escalation of certain proposed 
transactions.  
Prior to proceeding to credit approval, the EDR reviews the proposed transaction’s compliance with the 
fossil fuel financing related commitments in the CBA Group E&S Framework, impact on the glidepath 
and/or exposure reporting for certain sectors, and any E&S reputational considerations. If a proposed 
transaction is considered compliant with the CBA Group fossil fuel financing related commitments, but 
requires further review, it is escalated to the CBA IB&M Commitments Committee.  
The CBA IB&M Commitments Committee (which is run by CBA IB&M in Australia) considers reputational 
risks and alignment of proposed transactions or business decisions with CBA Group’s strategy and values. 
The Committee considers the expectations of broader stakeholder groups and incorporates CBA Group’s 
‘Should We?’ test. E&S-related matters escalated to the CBA IB&M Commitments Committee are also 
noted at the CBA Group Executive Leadership Team E&S Committee, which meets monthly (with the 
exception of December). 
The ‘Should We’ test ensures decisions made within CBA Group align with the CBA Group values and 
expectations. It involves asking a series of questions to determine whether an action is appropriate and 
ethical.

Training  
CBA NZ monitors IB&M NZ staff completion of mandatory E&S training, to ensure it is completed on time. 
This includes training on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Risk Fundamentals, and the 
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Tool, which helps staff to understand the key steps to 
completing ESG due diligence, and how to identify material ESG risks for the clients, and to assess the 
client’s ESG risk mitigation strategies. This training and the ESG Tool include climate-related risks. 
 
Assignment of roles and processes, and frequency of engagement with the governance body  
Escalation of climate-related issues from the IB&M NZ FRC & IB&M NZ NFRC is on an as required basis.  
• 
Any issues that require escalation from the IB&M NZ FRC may be escalated to the CBA IB&M FRC, 
the Market Risk Committee, the CBA IB&M Loan Loss Committee, or the CBA IB&M NFRC as 
required. Further escalation from these forums may be to the CBA Group FRC, and then if 
necessary to the CBA Board Risk & Compliance Committee.  
• 
Any issues requiring escalation from the IB&M NZ NFRC may be escalated to the Global Markets 
NFRC or the CBA IB&M NFRC. Further escalation from these forums may be to the CBA Group 
NFRC or the E&S Committee, and then if necessary to the CBA Board Risk & Compliance 
Committee. 
In addition, information relevant to CBA Group’s climate-related metrics (e.g. sector-level financed 
emissions targets) and policies (compliance with E&S Framework) are collated by CBA Group centrally, and 
included as part of the biannual E&S Update to the CBA Group Board. One of the metrics incorporates 
data from across IB&M (including IB&M NZ): ’Institutional: Percentage of portfolio exposed to clients with 
high residual climate transition risk (IB&M only, excl. Banks, Sovereigns and Agri, quarterly’’. The metrics 
are reported via the CBA Group Financial Risk ‘Risk Appetite Statement’ Dashboard to the CBA Group 
Executive Leadership Team Financial Risk Committee, which endorses the pack before presenting to the 
CBA Group Board.

Scenario analysis undertaken 
Our methodology 
Climate scenario analysis is a rapidly evolving field, with global scenarios regularly produced and updated. 
CBA Group uses assumptions and inputs drawing from global climate scenarios produced by parties such 
as the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS).  
CBA NZ management, along with CBA Group subject-matter experts, conducted a qualitative, standalone 
assessment of climate-related risks and opportunities under three scenarios, drawing from the NGFS 
scenarios. The purpose of the assessment was to further our understanding of the key risks facing CBA 
NZ, and to meet the disclosure requirements of the NZ CS 1. No external partners or stakeholders were 
involved in the assessment. While this process commenced during the financial year, it was completed 
after 30 June 2024 as this statement was being prepared.  
In 2024, CBA Group conducted certain scenario analyses drawing from the Network for Greening the 
Financial System (NGFS) scenarios. The NGFS scenarios are used by many global banks for the purposes 
of scenario analysis, and inform the scenarios CBA’s E&S Action Group has selected for the purpose of 
scenario analysis in 2024. In New Zealand, some banks have drawn from a set of scenarios developed by 
the New Zealand Banking Association (NZBA) for the purposes of scenario analysis. CBA NZ is not a 
member of the NZBA, and accordingly was not involved in the preparation of those scenarios. CBA NZ 
drew from a set of global scenarios consistent with those set at CBA Group level to inform the qualitative 
standalone assessment. 
In 2024, the CBA Group Environmental & Social Action Group approved a range of scenarios for the 
purposes of scenario analysis. To conduct the exercise for CBA NZ, CBA NZ management and the CBA 
Group Climate Analytics team used the CBA Group’s approved scenario analysis as a starting point. They 
reviewed and agreed on three NGFS scenarios for the CBA NZ Group assessment: “Net Zero (1.5°C)”, 
“Disorderly Transition (~1.8°C)”, and “Current Policies (>3°C)” scenarios. The three scenarios present 
plausible and appropriately severe outcomes, are consistent with market practices, and have detailed 
sector and geographic data readily available. Drawing from these global scenarios, CBA’s Group Climate 
Analytics team drew out possible implications relevant to CBA NZ’s operations and lending portfolios. 
These implications then informed a qualitative assessment of climate risks and opportunities relevant to 
the CBA NZ lending portfolio.  CBA NZ Group management then considered implications for CBA NZ’s 
strategy. The CBA Group Board was not involved in the scenario analysis for CBA NZ, and no modelling has 
been undertaken.

Transition risks and opportunities in higher-risk sectors 
Energy sector: faces significant transition risks from the need to decarbonise the energy supply and 
demand. The sector has opportunities to invest in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and low-carbon 
technologies. 
Agriculture sector: faces possible changes in consumer preferences, market access, and environmental 
standards. The agriculture sector accounts for about 50% of New Zealand’s GHG emissions in terms of 
CO2-equivalent, and the current government has advised that the sector will not come under the 
Emissions Trading Scheme before 2030.  The sector has opportunities to adapt to the changing 
conditions, mitigate its emissions, and provide ecosystem services. 
Transport sector: is heavily dependent on road transport and fossil fuels. The transport sector faces 
transition risks from the shift to low-carbon modes, fuels, and vehicles. The sector has opportunities to 
improve its efficiency, accessibility, and sustainability, and to leverage new technologies and innovations. 
Infrastructure sector: faces transition risks from the need to align the infrastructure planning, design, and 
investment with the low-carbon and climate-resilient objectives and standards. The sector has 
opportunities to enhance its performance, reliability, and sustainability, and to contribute to the climate 
transition and adaptation. 
Property sector: faces transition risks from the need to improve the property design, construction, and 
management to meet the low-carbon and climate-resilient standards and expectations. The sector has 
opportunities to increase its efficiency, quality, and sustainability, and to benefit from the green building

Group Climate Risk Materiality Assessment approach  
CBA Group, including CBA NZ, uses a range of techniques to help identify and assess climate-related risks. 
CBA Group continues to mature its environmental risk management approach in line with evolving industry 
standards. This year CBA Group completed a Group Climate Risk Materiality Assessment (CRMA) which 
enhances its assessment of climate-related risks by assessing the climate impacts of two scenarios on 
each of the Bank’s material risk types over the current, short, medium and long term.  The CRMA and 
various scenario analyses help identify the potential climate-related risks and impacts to CBA Group and to 
our customers, people and communities.  
CBA NZ is included in the scope of the CRMA, as the CRMA includes CBA IB&M. The CRMA acknowledges 
that the impacts of climate change are uncertain, and consequently, risks to CBA NZ may also vary 
substantially depending on external factors such as the nature and speed of action from government and 
industries to address climate change impacts. Anticipated effects were assessed across three time 
horizons:  
• 
Short term (~3 years) to align with CBA Group’s strategic planning cycle; 
• 
Medium term (~10 years) to align with the 2030 timeframe for CBA Group’s interim emissions 
targets; and 
• 
Long term (~30 years) 
The risk ratings for each risk type arising from climate change impacts were assessed using CBA Group’s 
risk assessment matrix, which uses a combination of likelihood and impact of the risk eventuating to arrive 
at a risk rating of either insignificant, low, medium, high or very high. 
The assessment of:  
• 
Likelihood ranges from ‘rare’ (<5% chance of occurring) through to ‘almost certain’ (>80% 
chance of occurring).  
• 
Impacts uses a combination of qualitative factors and financial measures. Qualitative factors 
consider impacts on customers, people and the environment; customer service and operations; 
reputation and brand; and legal and regulatory compliance. The financial impacts range from 
negligible ≤$10 million; minor >$10 million; moderate >$30 million; major >$120 million or 
severe >$500 million  
For example, a medium risk could arise from a >5% likelihood of an impact between $30 million to $120 
million; or a <5% likelihood of an impact between $120 million to $500 million. The assessment of each 
risk reflects the impact on the Bank for the year in which the scenario occurs, rather than reflecting the 
cumulative impacts over all time horizons. Additionally, when considering impacts for future time horizons 
under these scenarios, the assessment did not assume any additional controls or actions are taken (other 
than those already in place) in response to the future risk drivers envisaged in these scenarios. Our 
intention is for the CRMA to be updated annually.

ESG risk assessment tool 
The ESG risk assessment tool plays an important role in IB&M NZ lending processes by assisting our 
bankers to:  
• 
Identify and assess the ESG risks (including climate-related risks) that IB&M NZ customers are 
exposed to.  
• 
Assess the mitigating actions that IB&M NZ customers take to manage their ESG risks.  
• 
Assess how lending to IB&M NZ customers aligns to the commitments made in the CBA Group 
E&S Framework.  
The ESG risk assessment tool is supported by a set of inherent risk ratings across industry ANZSIC codes 
for ten key focus areas: climate and energy, climate physical risk, water, pollution, biodiversity, human 
rights, labour rights and modern slavery, Indigenous rights, workplace health and safety, and anti-
corruption and governance. The tool also includes specific questions aimed at assessing whether lending 
to a customer is aligned to the commitments in CBA Group’s E&S Framework. CBA Group continues to 
enhance the control environment for completing ESG risk assessments.  
The tool directs bankers to obtain appropriate business and credit risk approvals. Decisions on lending 
transactions may be escalated to senior management or business unit governance committees, if the 
assessment requires further review against the E&S Framework or other ESG risk indicators. These 
escalation pathways support bankers to make risk-based decisions that consider potential ESG issues 
(including climate-related risks).  
For corporate lending decisions in IB&M NZ that involve transactions in sensitive sectors, additional 
mandatory questions are required to be answered as part of the ESG assessment, including targeted 
climate transition questions assigned to select customers in fossil fuel sectors.  
For relevant project finance transactions, IB&M NZ follows the Equator Principles process requirements. 
The ESG risk assessment tool is required to be used for all transactions in IB&M NZ.  
Under the Group ESG Credit Standard, ESG risk assessments must be completed for IB&M NZ clients at: 
• 
Onboarding of new clients 
• 
New funding requests 
• 
Annual credit reviews  
• 
Material credit events (e.g. change in lending terms or covenants, client default, etc). 
The ESG risk assessment tool does not break climate-related risks and impacts down by time horizon. It 
requires staff to consider physical and transition risks that have occurred in the past, and those that may 
be expected to impact the client in the future. It also focuses on determining how clients intend to manage 
those likely impacts.

retail customers and lays a foundation for monitoring the ESG risk profile of all credit portfolios, including

Risk and control self-assessments 
Risk and control self-assessments (RCSAs) are used by CBA Group (including IB&M NZ) to identify and 
evaluate risks and the effectiveness of controls in place to manage those risks. RCSAs help us to identify 
risks in a consistent manner and understand the strength of our control environment. IB&M NZ has an 
‘Environmental Strategic’ risk which includes climate-related risks and impacts. IB&M NZ reviews and 
updates all risks in the profile at least annually, or more frequently when a trigger event occurs (e.g. 
legislative change). 
The RCSA does not break climate-related risks and impacts down by time horizon. The RCSA is reviewed 
at least annually and requires staff to consider the physical and transition risks that have occurred in the 
last few years, and those that may be expected to impact CBA Group (including IB&M NZ) in the future, as 
well as the impacts these risks could cause, and the controls in place to mitigate them. 
 
Compliance self-assessments 
A compliance self-assessment (CSA) is a process where Business Profile Owners (BPOs) evaluate the 
adequacy of key controls and compliance arrangements to ensure ongoing compliance with obligations. In 
CBA Group (including IB&M NZ) outcomes are recorded at the obligation summary level. The assessment 
considers new and changed regulations and legislation and is supported by advice from Line 2 
Compliance. IB&M NZ has an obligation summary for ‘Maintain adequate capabilities and processes for 
managing climate and environmental risks’ which captures climate-related legislation within the Financial 
Markets Conduct Act (FMCA), Financial Markets Conduct (Climate-related Disclosures) Regulations, 
Financial Reporting Act, NZ CS 1, NZ CS 2 and NZ CS 3. 
The CSAs do not break climate-related obligations down by time horizon. They are reviewed at least once 
every two years (or more often as required) and require staff to consider any change in the obligations or 
our compliance with them, as well as the controls and compliance arrangements in place to meet them, 
and any issues or incidents relating to the design or operation of these controls.
